title: High in Life and in Death
intro: Ibn Khallikan records that Adud al-Dawla had the vizier Ibn Baqiyya killed in 367 AH (978 CE) and his body displayed at Bab al-Taq in Baghdad. Abu al-Hasan al-Anbari addresses him still hanging there. His outstretched arms recover the gesture of giving, and the spectators become a congregation. Even the customary prayer for rain on a grave has to be thought out anew for this man.

translation: High in life and in death as well.
Truly, you are one of the wonders.
1.sharh: A single word for height covers two very different sights, a man eminent in office and a body raised above the crowd. The manner of his death only gradually comes into view.

translation: The people standing around you look
like delegations come for gifts in your days of giving.
2.sharh: The bystanders fall into a familiar arrangement around the former vizier. Imagining them as petitioners lets him occupy the centre again as the man with something to give.

translation: You might be standing there to preach to them,
and every one of them standing for prayer.
3.sharh: The same crowd can be seen from another angle. The raised figure now has a preacher’s place, with people on their feet before him. The Arabic brings the words for gifts and prayer very close in sound across the two verses.

translation: You hold out both hands to welcome them,
as you held them out to offer gifts.
4.sharh: The outstretched arms are the most conspicuous feature of the displayed body. By addressing the dead man as the one who extends them, the mourner gives a forced position the intention of a host.

translation: When earth’s belly proved too narrow
to enfold your greatness after death,
5.sharh: “Belly” makes the earth a body that should be able to take another body inside. What defeats it is the dead man’s greatness. The sentence leaves his resting place open until the next verse.

translation: they made the open air your grave
and took windblown dust for your shroud.
6.sharh: A grave ought to enclose the dead and a shroud to cover them. Here all the covering the open air can supply is what the wind carries past. The attempt to give him burial honours keeps his exposure visible.

translation: Such is your place in people’s hearts, you pass the night
watched by guards and trusted keepers.
7.sharh: The guards belong to the machinery of punishment. Read as signs of their charge’s value, their very presence testifies to the dead man’s standing. The judgement begins inside people’s minds.

translation: Fires are kindled around you at night.
So it was in the days of your life.
8.sharh: Firelight would once have guided a caller to his house at night. A guard’s fire can cast precisely the light the mourner remembers from a place of hospitality.

translation: You rode a mount that Zayd before you
had mounted in years gone by.
9.sharh: The mount is the timber bearing his body. Zayd ibn Ali, whose body was likewise displayed after his death, gives the bereaved a predecessor they can name with honour.

translation: There is a precedent in that to comfort you
and put your enemies’ taunts beyond your reach.
10.sharh: A listener who honours Zayd cannot take the manner of Ibn Baqiyya’s death as proof of disgrace. The mourner gives his opponents a case against which to test their jeers.

translation: Before your timber I never saw a tree trunk
able to take noble deeds in its arms.
11.sharh: The wood acquires the embracing arms the body itself cannot move. It holds a whole lifetime’s acts of generosity in the space one man’s body occupies.

translation: You wronged calamities, and they rose in anger.
It was calamities’ vengeance that killed you.
12.sharh: Saving others makes him an offender from the point of view of misfortune. Calamities now behave like a family with a blood debt to collect, which gives his fate a past as well as a cause.

translation: You used to shelter us from fortune’s turns.
Now it comes back to press its claims against you.
13.sharh: “Us” makes the mourner a beneficiary of the protection he describes. Time returns like an injured claimant and seeks out the very person who once stood between it and its victims.

translation: Your own age has counted the kindness
you showed us among its gravest sins.
14.sharh: A trial is implicit in the language of grave offences. The people who received the kindness can supply its true name even while the age that condemned the giver enters it on the charge sheet.

translation: You were good fortune for a whole company.
When you went, ill stars scattered them.
15.sharh: The vocabulary is that of favourable and inauspicious stars. The evidence of a changed sky is on the ground, in a group of people who can no longer hold together.

translation: There is a burning ache for you deep in my heart.
Running tears ease it.
16.sharh: The company has dispersed, leaving a single speaker with a bodily sensation. Running water offers an exact counter to the heat within, though the verb promises only a measure of relief.

translation: If I had the power to discharge
what I owe you, every obligation,
17.sharh: Duty is twice expressed, as something laid upon him and as the other man’s rightful due. The conditional hangs over the line ending before he can say what adequate payment would look like.

translation: I would fill the earth with rhymed verse
and wail in it in my own way, apart from the mourners.
18.sharh: The same earth that could not contain this man would be filled with verse. Poetry would carry a single mourner’s voice farther than the ritual lament he hears around him.

translation: Yet I school myself to bear your loss,
for fear of being counted among offenders.
19.sharh: The political risk reaches even the person who mourns. After imagining a lament loud enough to fill the earth, he describes the self-discipline required to keep speaking at all.

translation: You have no grave for me to wish rain upon.
You lie exposed to every downpour.
20.sharh: To ask for rain on someone’s grave is a traditional blessing. Here the dead man has no patch of earth to bless, and every shower already falls directly on him. The formula needs a different object.

translation: May the Merciful greet you time and again
with mercies that come morning and evening.
21.sharh: Mercy can reach the person wherever his body lies. Morning and evening make its coming a repeated visit, a counterpart to the delegations that once gathered around him.

1.1.1.head: عُلُوّ
1.1.1.meaning: Height, of rank in life and of the body above the crowd in death.

2.2.1-2.head: وُفود النَّدى
2.2.1-2.meaning: “Delegations of bounty”, groups arriving to ask a generous patron for gifts.

2.2.4.head: صِلَة
2.2.4.meaning: Gifts or grants to those who come to a patron.

3.1.4.head: خَطيب
3.1.4.meaning: A preacher addressing a congregation. The man’s position above the crowd calls to mind the preacher standing on a pulpit.

5.2.2.head: عُلا
5.2.2.meaning: Lofty standing, imagined as something too large for a grave.

6.1.1.head: أَصارَ
6.1.1.meaning: They made one thing into another, here turning air into a grave.

6.2.4.head: سافِيَة
6.2.4.meaning: Winds that sweep dust along and scatter it.

7.1.5.head: رَعى
7.1.5.meaning: To be watched over through the night.

8.1.3.head: نار
8.1.3.meaning: Fires, which can mark either a watch or a welcome.

9.1.2.head: مَطِيَّة
9.1.2.meaning: A riding animal, here the wood that bears the body.

9.1.5.head: زَيد
9.1.5.meaning: Zayd ibn Ali, grandson of Husayn. He was killed in the uprising at Kufa in 122 AH (740 CE), and his body was displayed afterwards.

10.1.4.meaning: Comfort taken from the example of someone who suffered a similar fate.

10.2.3.head: تَعيير
10.2.3.meaning: Reproaching someone with what is held to disgrace them.

11.1.4.head: جِذع
11.1.4.meaning: A tree trunk, used here for the timber on which the body hangs.

12.2.3.head: ثَأر
12.2.3.meaning: Vengeance exacted for an earlier injury or killing.

13.1.4-5.head: صَرف الدَّهر
13.1.4-5.meaning: “A turn of time”, a reversal of fortune.

13.2.4.head: تِرَة
13.2.4.meaning: Outstanding claims for injuries suffered, especially blood debts.

15.1.3.head: سَعد
15.1.3.meaning: Good fortune or a star held to bring it.

15.2.3.head: مُنحِسَة
15.2.3.meaning: Ill-omened influences, particularly the stars thought to bring misfortune.

16.1.1.head: غَليل
16.1.1.meaning: A burning thirst or ache, here the inward pain of loss.

17.2.1.head: فَرض
17.2.1.meaning: A binding obligation owed to the dead man.

18.2.4.head: نائِحَة
18.2.4.meaning: A woman who leads or voices a funeral lament.

19.2.5.head: جانٍ
19.2.5.meaning: People held guilty of an offence. Public mourning might itself be treated as one.

20.2.2.head: نُصب
20.2.2.meaning: Directly in the path of something, without cover.

20.2.3-4.head: هَطل الهاطِلات
20.2.3-4.meaning: The pouring rain of cloud after rain cloud.

21.1.4.meaning: In succession, one blessing following another.

21.2.2-3.head: غَوادٍ رائِحات
21.2.2-3.meaning: “Going out early and returning late”, blessings pictured as visitors through the day.
